description: Correlation, cause and the everyday choices linked to long-term health.
content_html:
What Makes a Disease Non-Communicable?

Not all diseases spread from person to person. Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) are conditions linked to how we live, the genes we inherit, and the environment around us. They include cardiovascular diseases, type 2 diabetes, many cancers, and obesity-related conditions. Because NCDs develop slowly and are often preventable, understanding their causes is one of the most powerful tools in public health.

Scientists and doctors identify risk factors — variables that increase the probability of a disease developing. Identifying risk factors guides both individual choices and government health policy. Crucially, a risk factor is not the same as a cause: this distinction is at the heart of how we reason about evidence in science.

Key Fact

Non-communicable diseases cannot be transmitted between people. They are associated with risk factors — genetic, lifestyle or environmental — that raise the probability of disease. Having a risk factor does not guarantee a person will develop the disease.

Correlation vs Causation — The Critical Distinction

One of the most important ideas in science is the difference between correlation and causation. When two things tend to change together — for example, people who smoke more tend to have higher rates of lung cancer — we say there is a correlation. But correlation alone does not tell us that one variable is causing the other.

A confounding variable is a hidden factor that might explain a correlation without there being a direct causal link. For example, people who sleep very little also tend to drink more caffeine, exercise less, and have higher stress levels — any of these could be the true driver of a health outcome. Good epidemiological research tries to control for confounding variables by studying very large populations and using statistical techniques to isolate individual factors.

Moving from correlation to causation requires multiple lines of evidence. Scientists look for: (1) a plausible biological mechanism — can we explain why the factor might cause the disease at the cellular or physiological level? (2) a dose-response relationship — does more of the risk factor lead to greater disease risk? (3) consistency across studies — do researchers in different countries with different populations reach the same conclusion? (4) temporality — does exposure to the factor come before the disease develops?

Peer review is essential here. Results from a single study — even a large one — are not treated as definitive until they have been scrutinised by independent scientists and replicated. This is why scientific consensus on lifestyle and health has built up gradually over decades, not from a single dramatic finding.

Major Risk Factors for Non-Communicable Diseases

Research has identified a range of lifestyle, genetic and environmental factors associated with increased risk of NCDs. These include diet, physical activity, alcohol consumption, smoking, and inherited genetic variants.

Diet and obesity: A diet consistently high in saturated fats and added sugars is associated with raised blood cholesterol, fatty deposits in arteries, and increased risk of cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes. Carrying excess body fat — particularly around the abdomen — is correlated with insulin resistance, hypertension, and cardiovascular risk. BMI is commonly used as a screening tool, though it does not distinguish between muscle and fat mass.

Physical inactivity: Regular physical activity is associated with lower blood pressure, improved blood sugar regulation, and a reduced risk of both cardiovascular disease and certain cancers. Inactivity is itself treated as a risk factor, not just the absence of benefit.

Smoking: Tobacco smoke contains hundreds of harmful chemicals. Long-term smoking is strongly and causally linked (multiple mechanisms established) to lung cancer, coronary heart disease, and stroke. It also raises the risk of several other cancers. Smoking during pregnancy is associated with lower birth weight in babies.

Alcohol: Excessive alcohol consumption over time is associated with liver disease, certain cancers, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease. There is a dose-response relationship — risk generally rises with increasing consumption. Occasional, moderate alcohol intake is harder to categorise from the evidence; confounding variables make this area complex.

Genetic Risk Factors

Some people inherit gene variants that raise their susceptibility to certain NCDs, regardless of lifestyle. For example, some individuals inherit a tendency to produce high levels of LDL cholesterol (LDL cholesterol), which increases cardiovascular risk even in people who eat a healthy diet. Similarly, certain gene variants increase the lifetime risk of developing type 2 diabetes.

Genetic risk factors interact with lifestyle factors — someone with a genetic predisposition to heart disease who also smokes and is physically inactive faces a compounded risk. This interaction makes it misleading to separate “genes” from “lifestyle” as if they operate independently. Understanding your genetic risk can motivate earlier lifestyle changes and more frequent health screening.

Key Fact

Genetic risk factors (inherited gene variants) and lifestyle risk factors (diet, exercise, smoking) interact. A person with a genetic predisposition to high LDL cholesterol faces even greater cardiovascular risk if their lifestyle also includes smoking or physical inactivity.

Cardiovascular Disease and Type 2 Diabetes

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) develops when fatty deposits accumulate inside artery walls — a process called atherosclerosis. These deposits narrow the artery, reducing blood flow and raising blood pressure. If a coronary artery becomes severely blocked, the heart muscle is starved of oxygen, leading to a heart attack. If a cerebral artery is blocked or bursts, the result is a stroke.

Type 2 diabetes involves the body’s cells becoming resistant to insulin. Blood glucose levels remain elevated after eating, putting stress on blood vessels and organs over time. It is strongly associated with obesity, physical inactivity and a diet high in refined sugars — but genetic factors also contribute. Unlike type 1 diabetes (an autoimmune condition), type 2 is often preventable through lifestyle changes, though it has a complex genetic component too.

Epidemiology is the scientific discipline that investigates the patterns of disease across populations. Epidemiologists use data from sources such as national health surveys, hospital records, and large cohort studies (which follow groups of people over many years) to identify which factors are associated with higher or lower rates of disease.

One challenge in epidemiology is the outlier. Within any large dataset, some individuals will have a very different outcome from the majority — a lifelong smoker who lives to a very old age, for example. Outliers do not disprove a risk factor; they remind us that risk is probabilistic, not deterministic. Scientists do not automatically remove outliers from data; they investigate whether there is a genuine reason (measurement error, a different genetic background) before deciding how to handle them.

Key Fact

Correlation means two variables tend to change together. Causation means one directly produces the other. To establish causation, scientists need a plausible biological mechanism, a dose-response relationship, consistency across studies, and evidence that exposure precedes disease.
exam_tip_html: Questions on lifestyle and disease often use data — a graph, table or study description — and ask you to “evaluate the evidence.” This is an Ideas about Science question: you must comment on the quality of the evidence (sample size, confounding variables, correlation vs causation) not just describe the data. Avoid writing “the data proves X” — instead write “the data suggests X, but confounding variables such as Y cannot be ruled out.” For 6-mark evaluate questions, always weigh both sides before reaching a conclusion.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Non-communicable diseases are linked to genetic, lifestyle and environmental risk factors rather than pathogens — they cannot be passed between people.
  • Correlation shows two variables change together; causation requires a biological mechanism, dose-response relationship and consistent replication before scientists accept it.
  • Major lifestyle risk factors for cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes include poor diet, physical inactivity, smoking and excessive alcohol — but genetic predisposition interacts with all of these.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a ‘risk factor’ for a non-communicable disease.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A factor that increases the probability (or chance/likelihood) of developing a disease [1]; it does not guarantee that the disease will occur [1].
Secure: A factor that makes it more likely that someone will develop a disease, but does not mean they definitely will.
Developing: Something that raises the chance of disease.
Emerging: A thing that causes disease.

practice_questions.text: A study followed 10,000 adults for 20 years. It found that those who exercised fewer than 3 hours per week had a higher rate of cardiovascular disease than those who exercised more. A journalist reported: ‘Lack of exercise proves to cause heart disease.’ Explain why this conclusion is not fully supported by the evidence.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies that the study shows a correlation, not causation [1]; explains that confounding variables (e.g. diet, smoking, genetic factors) may account for the difference [1]; notes that one study is insufficient — findings need to be replicated [1]; recognises a plausible mechanism would need to be established [1]; conclusion is clearly stated and evidence weighed [1].
Secure: States correlation vs causation [1]; identifies at least one confounding variable [1]; recognises replication is needed [1]; one further valid point.
Developing: Identifies correlation vs causation or one confounding variable, with limited further development.
Emerging: States the study is not proof, with no scientific reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Explain how both genetic and lifestyle risk factors can contribute to the development of type 2 diabetes.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Genetic factors: some individuals inherit gene variants that increase insulin resistance or reduce insulin production [1]; Lifestyle factors: diet high in refined sugars / physical inactivity / obesity associated with insulin resistance [1]; interaction: genetic predisposition is amplified by lifestyle factors, compounding risk [1]; conclusion that neither acts in isolation [1].
Secure: One genetic factor [1] and one lifestyle factor [1] described; some reference to interaction.
Developing: Names risk factors without explaining their mechanisms.
Emerging: Names diabetes without linking to causes.

practice_questions.text: A researcher wants to investigate whether high BMI is a risk factor for cardiovascular disease. Describe how she could design an epidemiological study to investigate this, including what data she would collect and how she would control for confounding variables.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Large cohort study with participants at different BMI levels [1]; collect cardiovascular disease rates over time [1]; control for confounding variables e.g. smoking status, diet, exercise, age [1]; large sample size to ensure statistical reliability [1].
Secure: Describes collecting BMI and CVD data [1]; identifies need to control confounders [1]; two further valid points.
Developing: Basic method described; limited discussion of controls.
Emerging: States she would collect health data, with no further detail.

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether the evidence that smoking causes lung cancer is stronger than evidence that eating saturated fat causes cardiovascular disease. Use your knowledge of how scientific evidence is evaluated.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Smoking-lung cancer: biological mechanism well-established (carcinogens in smoke damage DNA in lung cells) [1]; dose-response relationship clear [1]; consistent across many studies and populations [1]; Saturated fat-CVD: plausible mechanism (raises LDL, promotes atherosclerosis) [1]; but confounding variables harder to control in dietary studies [1]; reasoned conclusion on relative strength of evidence [1].
Secure: At least two valid points on each side; conclusion present.
Developing: Valid points on one side only.
Emerging: States one causes disease without evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Give one reason why an outlier in a dataset showing the relationship between alcohol consumption and liver disease should not automatically be removed from the analysis.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Outliers are part of the real data; removing them without justification would bias the results / they may represent genuine variation in the population / their cause should be investigated first (accept any valid equivalent).

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following best describes a non-communicable disease?
options: A disease caused by a pathogen that spreads between people
A disease linked to lifestyle, genetic or environmental factors that cannot be transmitted
A disease that only affects older people
A disease caused exclusively by inherited gene mutations

knowledge_checks.q: A researcher finds that people who eat more fish have lower rates of heart disease. What is the most important reason why this does not prove that eating fish prevents heart disease?
options: The sample size was too small
Confounding variables such as overall diet quality or exercise levels may explain the pattern
The correlation is negative rather than positive
The study was not peer reviewed

knowledge_checks.q: BMI is calculated from a person’s height and weight and is used to assess whether body _____ is in a healthy range.
A _____ variable is a hidden factor that influences both an apparent cause and an apparent effect, creating a false impression of a direct link.
Match each term to its correct description.
right: A direct relationship where one variable produces an observed effect
A statistical relationship where two variables tend to change together
A factor that raises the probability of developing a disease

flashcard_questions.a: A disease that cannot be transmitted between people, linked to lifestyle, genetic or environmental factors.
A variable that increases the probability of developing a disease without guaranteeing it will occur.

flashcard_questions.q: Correlation shows two variables change together. What additional evidence is needed to establish causation?
flashcard_questions.a: A plausible biological mechanism, dose-response relationship, consistency across studies, and correct timing of exposure.
A hidden factor that influences both the apparent cause and effect, creating a false impression of a direct link.

flashcard_questions.q: What does BMI measure, and what is its limitation?
flashcard_questions.a: It estimates healthy weight from height and mass, but cannot distinguish between muscle and fat tissue.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the process by which fatty deposits accumulate inside artery walls.
What is the difference between type 1 and type 2 diabetes?
flashcard_questions.a: Type 1 is autoimmune; type 2 involves insulin resistance, often linked to lifestyle and genetic factors.

flashcard_questions.q: How does LDL cholesterol contribute to cardiovascular disease?
flashcard_questions.a: High LDL levels promote fatty deposit build-up inside arteries, narrowing them and restricting blood flow.

flashcard_questions.q: Epidemiology is the study of _____ of disease across populations.
flashcard_questions.a: Epidemiology studies the patterns, distribution, and causes of disease in populations to inform public health.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do scientists not automatically remove outliers from health data?
flashcard_questions.a: Outliers may represent genuine variation; their cause should be investigated before any decision to exclude them.

flashcard_questions.q: How do genetic and lifestyle risk factors interact for type 2 diabetes?
flashcard_questions.a: A genetic predisposition is amplified by lifestyle factors like obesity and inactivity, compounding overall risk.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a dose-response relationship show in evidence for causation?
flashcard_questions.a: Greater exposure to the risk factor leads to greater disease risk, strengthening the case for a causal link.

glossary_terms.definition: A disease that cannot be passed from one person to another, caused by genetic, lifestyle or environmental factors rather than pathogens.
A factor that increases the probability of developing a disease; it does not guarantee the disease will occur.
A statistical relationship between two variables, where changes in one tend to accompany changes in the other, without implying causation.
A direct relationship where one factor produces an observed effect, established through multiple lines of evidence including mechanism and dose-response.
A third variable that influences both the apparent cause and apparent effect, which can create a false impression of a direct link between two variables.
Body Mass Index — a measure calculated from height and weight used to assess whether body weight is in a healthy range, though it cannot distinguish muscle from fat.
A group of conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels, including coronary heart disease, heart attack and stroke, often linked to atherosclerosis.
A metabolic condition where the body's cells do not respond properly to insulin, leading to elevated blood glucose levels, associated with obesity and genetic factors.
A type of lipoprotein that carries cholesterol in the blood; high levels are associated with a greater risk of fatty deposits building up in arteries.
The branch of medicine that studies the distribution, patterns and determinants of health and disease in populations, often using large-scale data.
